title: Ind AS 115 "Revenue from Contracts with Customers"
outcomes: Identify contracts and distinct performance obligations.
Determine the transaction price including variable consideration.
Allocate the price and recognise revenue over time or at a point in time.
Account for contract costs, principal-agent issues, licences and concessions.

meta.exam_tip: Write the five steps as headings in every revenue answer.

concepts.title: Steps 1 and 2: contract and performance obligations
body: Ind AS 115 uses a five-step model: identify the contract; identify performance obligations; determine the transaction price; allocate it; recognise revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied.

A contract exists when it is approved and parties are committed, rights and payment terms are identifiable, it has commercial substance, and collection is probable. Contracts are combined when negotiated as a package; modifications are separate contracts if they add distinct goods at stand-alone prices.

A performance obligation is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service (or a series of substantially the same distinct items). A good is distinct if the customer can benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and the promise is separately identifiable within the contract.
concepts.analogy: Five steps, always in order — most errors start in step 2.
concepts.work: A software licence with essential customisation may be one obligation.

concepts.title: Step 3: transaction price and variable consideration
body: The transaction price is the consideration the seller expects to earn for handing over the promised goods or services, excluding amounts collected for third parties such as GST.

Variable consideration (discounts, rebates, refunds, incentives, penalties) is estimated using expected value or most likely amount, and included only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal will not occur when uncertainty resolves. Expected returns create a refund liability and a right-to-recover asset.

A significant financing component adjusts the price for time value (practical expedient where the gap is one year or less). Non-cash consideration is at fair value. Consideration payable to a customer reduces revenue unless for a distinct good or service.
concepts.analogy: Price is what you expect to earn, trimmed by the reversal constraint.
concepts.work: A volume rebate likely to be earned reduces revenue now.

concepts.title: Steps 4 and 5: allocation and satisfaction
body: The price is allocated to each obligation in proportion to stand-alone selling prices, estimated by adjusted market assessment, expected cost plus margin, or residual approach (only in limited cases). Discounts and variable consideration are allocated to specific obligations only when criteria are met.

Revenue is recognised when control passes. Over time if: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits; the entity's work creates or enhances an asset the customer controls; or the asset cannot be redirected to another use and the seller can legally demand payment for performance so far. Otherwise at a point in time, using indicators such as right to payment, legal title, physical possession, risks and rewards, and acceptance.
Progress is measured by output methods (units delivered, milestones) or input methods (costs incurred), excluding costs that do not depict performance such as wasted materials or uninstalled goods.
concepts.analogy: Allocate by stand-alone prices; recognise as control moves.
concepts.work: A building on the customer's land is satisfied over time.

concepts.title: Special topics: costs, agents, licences, concessions
body: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract (e.g. sales commissions) are capitalised if expected to be recovered (expedient: expense if amortisation period is a year or less). Costs to fulfil are capitalised if they relate directly to a contract, create resources used in future, and are recoverable. These assets are amortised on a basis consistent with the transfer of goods and tested for impairment.

Principal versus agent: an entity is a principal if it controls the good before transfer (indicators: primary responsibility, inventory risk, pricing discretion) and recognises gross revenue; an agent recognises only its commission.

Other topics: licences (right to access — over time; right to use — point in time); bill-and-hold, consignment, repurchase agreements, customer options for additional goods (material rights), warranties (assurance vs service-type), and service concession arrangements under Appendix D, where the operator recognises a financial asset or an intangible asset depending on who bears demand risk.
concepts.analogy: Capitalise costs that win or fulfil contracts; decide gross or net by control.
concepts.work: A travel portal selling flights as an agent records only its commission.

illustrations.title: A phone with a service plan
illustrations.q: Volt Telecom sells a handset with a 12-month service plan for ₹35,000 paid upfront on 1 January. Stand-alone prices: handset ₹30,000, service plan ₹12,000. The handset is delivered on 1 January. How much revenue is recognised by 31 March?

illustrations.title: Variable price and over-time revenue
illustrations.q: (a) Fresh Mills sells 1,000 units; the final price depends on a market index: ₹100 (60% likely), ₹90 (30%), ₹80 (10%). Using expected value, what is the transaction price, assuming it is highly probable no significant reversal will occur? (b) Brick Builders has a fixed-price contract of ₹200 lakh; costs incurred ₹60 lakh, further costs ₹90 lakh expected; control passes over time. Compute progress and revenue to date.

jobs.title: Revenue policy review
jobs.situation: A SaaS company sells subscriptions with setup and support.
steps: Capitalise sales commissions and amortise them.
jobs.takeaway: Contract terms decide the pattern; document every judgement.

viva.q: List the five steps of Ind AS 115.
viva.model: Identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate the price, and recognise revenue as obligations are satisfied.

viva.q: What is the constraint on variable consideration?
viva.model: Include it only to the extent it is highly probable that revenue already booked will escape any significant reversal later.

viva.q: When is revenue recognised over time?
viva.model: When the customer receives and consumes benefits as performed, controls the asset being created, or the asset has no alternative use with an enforceable right to payment.

viva.q: How do you decide principal or agent?
viva.model: By assessing whether the entity controls the good or service before transfer, using indicators like primary responsibility, inventory risk and pricing discretion.

viva.q: How does a service concession operator account for its right?
viva.model: As a financial asset if it has an unconditional right to receive cash from the grantor, or as an intangible asset if it has a right to charge users.

cases.title: Pinnacle Machines Ltd.
cases.case: Pinnacle Machines Ltd. sells a machine for ₹90 lakh with installation (simple, available from others) and a 2-year service-type warranty beyond the standard assurance. Stand-alone prices: machine ₹80 lakh, installation ₹10 lakh, extended warranty ₹10 lakh. Its sales staff earn 2% commission on each contract.

mcqs.explain: Machine, installation and service-type warranty are distinct. In practice: assurance warranty is not separate.
mcqs.topic: Steps 1 and 2: contract and performance obligations

mcqs.q: Revenue allocated to the machine (₹ lakh):
Revenue for the extended warranty is recognised:
mcqs.explain: A stand-ready obligation satisfied over time. In practice: straight-line often fits.

options: Capitalised as a cost to obtain the contract, if recoverable
mcqs.explain: An incremental cost of obtaining the contract. In practice: amortise with the revenue pattern.
